summary: Rutgers and Boston University release Collider-Bench: 10 tasks from four CMS supersymmetry searches in which a coding agent must turn a public paper into a simulation and selection pipeline and submit binned signal yields. Scoring is a relative L2 distance against hidden reference yields, plus a Claude Opus 4.6 provenance judge. Six agent CLIs are run three times with a 2.5-hour budget.

claims.claim: On average no agent reliably beats the physicist-in-the-loop solution
claims.evidence: §4.2 and the conclusion: autonomous agents pass only a subset of tasks under tau=0.33, defined as the worst relative L2 of the supervised baseline. Table 2 gives per-task mean±sigma for six agents; several cells sit well above 0.33 (for example Opus 4.7 is 0.44±0.26 and 0.38±0.63 on two SUS-16-047 tasks) while others are near 0.1. The supervised baseline is Opus 4.7 plus a human expert, so the gap mixes human judgment with the strongest model. The pass rule is 'match the weakest supervised task', not 'beat the physicist on that task'.

claims.claim: Histogram metrics score fidelity without a hand-written rubric, and a provenance judge catches fabrication
claims.evidence: Relative L2 is defined and applied. §4.5: over 364 judged runs the Opus 4.6 judge marks 87% Passed, 6% Failed, 6% Fabricated, with fabrication concentrated in Haiku 4.5, DeepSeek-V4, and GPT-5.4-mini. Appendix E says the judge sees a 50k-character log extract, not the full trace, and may recover unsubmitted bin values and trigger a re-score. No human agreement on the labels.

claims.claim: Shape reconstruction is easier than absolute yield, and the two failure modes separate
claims.evidence: §4.3: agents do better on normalized shape than on full yields; Fig. 3(c) is described as a weak correlation between shape error and normalization error. The shape-task rerun (Fig. 3(d)) is strongly correlated with simulation-task shape error for the best agents. No numeric correlation is printed in the text.

claims.claim: Cost is reported per agent and forms a frontier with accuracy
claims.evidence: Table 4, mean±sigma over the 10 simulation tasks: Opus 4.7 about $14.21±4.56 and 0.37M billed tokens; GPT-5.5 about $10.71 with 16.46M tokens; Haiku about $1.09; DeepSeek-V4 about $0.89. Fig. 2(b) plots Acc at tau=0.33 against cost. List prices, Spring 2026.

patterns.note: Each task forces the agent to read a paper and fill omitted implementation details. That is the benchmark's difficulty, not a comparison of discovery strategies.

The provenance judge is a separate model and does not set the L2 score, which is good. It is unvalidated, same-family with the Claude Code agents, sees only a truncated log, and can change the submitted histogram before rescoring.
New 10-task physics benchmark with hidden yields, three runs, and a released sandbox. It does not yet support a claim that this task family ranks coding agents for software work.
Dollar and token cost are reported (Table 4) and not used as an optimization target.

methodology.sample: 10 simulation tasks from four CMS 13 TeV searches (35.9 fb^-1), plus a matched shape-only suite. Tasks kept only if a domain expert could recast them on the public toolchain.
methodology.baselines: Physicist supervising Claude Code Opus 4.7 on the same tools. Agents are not compared with each other under one scaffold.
methodology.models: Claude Code: Opus 4.7, Sonnet 4.6, Haiku 4.5. Codex: GPT-5.5, GPT-5.4-mini. ForgeCode: DeepSeek-V4. Judge: Claude Opus 4.6.
methodology.variance: Three independent runs; Table 2 reports mean ± 1 sigma. Some cells are single runs. Fig. 3 shows best-of-three.
methodology.ablations: Shape tasks drop absolute normalization. Delphes removed for GPT-5.5 only (Appendix D.1), with a qualitative task-dependent result.
methodology.contamination_controls: Reference yields hidden from the agent, but the source papers contain the published numbers. The judge is supposed to flag copies and hardcoded histograms. No pretraining-contamination check.
methodology.languages: Python plus HEP CLI tools (event generation, Delphes). Not a software repo and not Java.

standards.artifacts: Code at github.com/dfaroughy/Collider-Bench and tasks on Hugging Face (Dariusfar/ColliderBench), with a containerized sandbox

biases.detail: Ten tasks, four papers, one experiment, one luminosity. The conclusion's 'six agents' omits that the ladder is three families on one scaffold each.
§3.2 keeps searches an expert can already recast with the public stack and drops analyses that need internal reconstruction.
Fabrication rates come from Opus 4.6 with no human audit, and the judge can rewrite the scored yields from the log.
tau=0.33 is the supervised baseline's worst error, so 'pass' means 'no worse than the weakest human-guided task', which the abstract compresses to 'does not beat the physicist'.
Published yields and selections are in the papers the agent is given. Copying them is a known failure mode the judge only partly covers.
Simulation CPU on 128 cores is not costed; only model list price is. The physicist baseline's human time is not reported.

coi.affiliations: Rutgers University (New High Energy Theory Center) and Boston University
coi.vendor_products_evaluated: Anthropic, OpenAI, and DeepSeek agent CLIs. No author model.
coi.funding: DOE grant DOE-SC0010008 and NERSC award HEPERCAP0027491
coi.detail: Academic benchmark. Vendors supply the agents under test; authors do not ship one.

verdict_reason: Off-topic. Collider-Bench measures whether agents can recast LHC searches, not software development, onboarding, or repository question answering. The three-run table is careful and the code is released, but ten survivorship-filtered tasks, a lenient threshold set by the human baseline, and an unvalidated judge that can change scores do not support a harness decision.
applicability: Do not use these rankings to choose a coding agent or a discovery workflow for the Java ingestion repos. The only transferable caution is generic and already expected: a numeric answer can look plausible when the pipeline was abandoned or the values were copied from the source document, so an exploration agent that cites a paper should show the command that produced the number. That caution is not measured here outside particle-physics simulation.
